generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, approaching an exam is one habit you bring to each module. You ask what the exam is for, find out whether it wants recall, essays or applied method, and plan revision to match. Across your degree, that single approach turns exams from stressful hurdles into a steady part of how you learn psychology.
generatedProse.worked-example: Two psychology students have a statistics exam in two weeks. One revises by rereading the lecture slides, without checking what the exam will actually ask. The other brings the three strands together. She sees the exam as a chance to understand the methods, finds out it is a technical exam on running and reading tests, and plans her time around the procedures she finds hardest. Her preparation is sharper, because she approached the exam as one practice rather than three separate steps.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, approaching an exam works best as one habit across your modules. You ask what the exam is for, match your revision to its type, and plan your time around the topics you find hardest. The whole approach, exam after exam, is what makes assessment feel manageable.

check.body: A student finds out her exam is an essay exam, treats it as a chance to build her thinking, and plans two weeks of revision around her weaker topics. What does this show?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following report improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first report, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next report.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using the feedback fed back into the next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following report improved: that is the cycle working.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student changed before the next report, not the old mark or the deadline.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Using the feedback fed back into the student's next round of learning and preparation, which is why the next report improved. The old mark cannot change and the deadline is not part of the cycle; feedback is not the end, it feeds the next turn.

_items.text: The whole approach at work: she used the purpose and the type to decide what to revise, then planned her time to match.
_items.feedback: Yes. Purpose, type and strategy are all there, working together.

_items.text: Only cramming, because she revised for two weeks.
_items.feedback: Spreading revision over two weeks is a strategy, not cramming.

_items.text: Only the exam type, because she found out it was an essay exam.
_items.feedback: She did more than name the type. She also planned revision to match it.

_items.text: Nothing useful, because the mark is all that counts.
_items.feedback: The mark is not the point here. Her approach is what the scenario shows.
